name: The “journey of a young architect” plots the complexity of the architectures a developer builds against the developer's experience. Select all correct statements.

answers.body: At first, learning architecture makes the developer build ever more complex architectures, until the curve reaches a peak of over-engineering.
answers.comment: L6, slides 2-9: The curve rises with experience to a peak before it drops.

answers.body: The peak is a necessary waypoint toward pragmatic architecture, so the lecture does not tell you to skip it.
answers.comment: L6, slide 10: The speaker says the peak is a necessary waypoint and only offers hints for later decisions.

answers.body: After the peak, experienced architects keep choosing the most complex architecture available, because complexity shows skill.
answers.comment: L6, slides 9-10: After the peak complexity drops to the amount the project actually needs.

answers.body: The peak is wasted effort and a developer should skip over-engineered architectures completely to reach pragmatic architecture faster.
answers.comment: L6, slide 10: The lecture calls the peak a necessary waypoint, not a mistake to skip.

name: Complexity of the architecture is compared with complexity of the problem being solved. Select all combinations that the lecture presents as a good fit.

answers.body: A simple app with a simple architecture.
answers.comment: L6, slide 14: Both complexities match, so there is no unnecessary overhead.

answers.body: A complex app with a complex architecture.
answers.comment: L6, slide 15: The architecture is strong enough for the problem it has to solve.

answers.body: A simple app with a complex architecture.
answers.comment: L6, slide 16: A mismatch – the app pays for layers and ceremony it does not need.

answers.body: A complex app with a simple architecture.
answers.comment: L6, slide 17: A mismatch – the structure cannot cope with the problem and breaks down as the app grows.

answers.body: One architecture chosen once and reused unchanged for the next projects, whatever the problem.
answers.comment: L6, slides 19-20: Architecture is a mosaic of decisions that should fit each problem, not one fixed choice.

name: A team of eight shares one codebase. Select all observations that suggest the code needs MORE structure.

answers.body: Merge conflicts keep appearing in a few “god” services or files.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: Frequent merge conflicts in god files are listed as a sign of too little structure.

answers.body: ORM and framework choices leak into the whole codebase, so the team feels locked in.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: Leaking framework/ORM choices signal missing boundaries.

answers.body: Trivial CRUD screens require many layers, DTOs and mappers, even for a simple field change.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: Ceremony overload signals too much structure, not too little.

answers.body: Simple features require touching 6+ layers or 10+ files.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: This is a sign of too much structure.

answers.body: 80% of test time goes to mocks and wiring, and brittle tests assert call sequences.
answers.comment: L6, slide 22: That is a sign of too much structure.

name: Architecture decisions were presented along three dimensions: code structure, deployment and problem modeling. Select all correct statements about their goals.

answers.body: Code structure and deployment share goals at different scales: high cohesion, low coupling, modules around business capabilities, replaceability.
answers.comment: L6, slides 21, 35: The two slides list identical goals; deployment is “just on bigger scale”.

answers.body: Problem modeling aims to capture business meaning, enforce business rules, prevent developer mistakes and improve testability.
answers.comment: L6, slide 46: These are the four goals listed for modeling.

answers.body: Each style differs along a single dimension, its complexity, and choosing an architecture means picking a point on one axis.
answers.comment: L6, slides 20-21, 35: Architecture is a mosaic of decisions; each style has many dimensions, not just complexity.

answers.body: Problem modeling aims to describe features as tables and DTOs, mirroring the database schema as closely as possible.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: Schema-driven thinking is a warning sign that more domain modeling is needed.

name: Three-layer architecture and clean architecture were compared. Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Three-layer architecture separates UI, business and data logic, suits CRUD-heavy apps and leads towards data-driven design.
answers.comment: L6, slide 23: These are the stated properties of three-layer architecture.

answers.body: Clean architecture focuses on solving business problems via use cases and tends to ignore how data is finally persisted.
answers.comment: L6, slides 24-26: Persistence is deliberately postponed.

answers.body: Clean architecture starts from the database tables and builds its use cases around them, putting data flow first.
answers.comment: L6, slide 24: The job in clean architecture is to solve business problems, not how data flows and is stored.

answers.body: In clean architecture, use cases call concrete repository classes directly and the business logic knows how data is stored.
answers.comment: L6, slide 27: Use cases request dependencies (ports) without caring about the implementation (adapters).

name: A clean-architecture use case AddTransactionUseCase(userId, amount, description, expiration) is handled by a handler that declares a transaction repository, a current-user provider and a mediator as dependencies; it loads the balance through a specification, throws an exception for a negative balance, creates the transaction, publishes a UserBalanceChanged notification and finally saves the transaction. Select all correct statements about what this illustrates.

answers.body: The handler just requests data through its dependencies without caring how it is retrieved.
answers.comment: L6, slide 31: Retrieval details stay behind the abstraction (port).

answers.body: The main focus is the business rule; the dependent action is triggered by publishing a notification instead of being performed inside the handler.
answers.comment: L6, slides 32-33: The handler is not bogged down with dependent actions.

answers.body: The handler opens the database connection and builds SQL itself and the business rule knows how data is stored.
answers.comment: L6, slides 26, 31: Ignoring persistence helps design better solutions.

answers.body: The handler calls the code that reacts to a balance change directly and the whole flow is visible in one place.
answers.comment: L6, slides 32-33: Dependent actions are published as notifications, not called directly.

answers.body: Saving comes first and the balance rule is checked afterwards, with persistence as the main focus.
answers.comment: L6, slide 34: Saving data is kind of an afterthought; the rule comes first.

name: Select all observations that indicate you need MORE separate applications (services) instead of one deployment.

answers.body: Many teams work side by side on the same codebase.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: Teams blocking each other is listed as a sign.

answers.body: Releases are slow or risky because one big deploy blocks everyone.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: A big deploy that blocks everyone is a listed sign.

answers.body: Different parts of the system need different scalability.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: Different scalability needs justify separate apps.

answers.body: There are too many services for the team size, and everyone touches everything.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: This signals that you need fewer separate apps.

answers.body: You end up deploying everything together anyway.
answers.comment: L6, slide 36: Always deploying everything together signals that you need fewer separate apps.

name: Which statements about the modular monolith are correct? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: It is designed as if it were a microservice architecture, but each service is not hosted separately, which spares the communication pain.
answers.comment: L6, slide 39: Microservice-style design without separate hosting.

answers.body: Each service is a separate module/project, and the shared messages (requests, notifications) are kept apart from the hidden implementation.
answers.comment: L6, slide 40: Implementation is kept separate from communication definitions.

answers.body: Each module is hosted as its own service from the start and modules talk to each other over the network.
answers.comment: L6, slide 39: Skipping separate hosting is the point of a modular monolith.

answers.body: It is a sign of good design when each module knows the others directly and communication stays simple.
answers.comment: L6, slide 41: Everyone knowing everyone is the “small village syndrome”, a sign of bad design.

answers.body: It is meant for projects that already have many teams and a single deployment is easier to split among them.
answers.comment: L6, slides 36, 68: It is a starting point when the future is unknown; many teams point towards more separate apps.

name: A module of a modular monolith may become a “satellite”. Select all correct statements.

answers.body: A module is a candidate when it is large and self-sufficient, carries much traffic needing more instances, or has its own team.
answers.comment: L6, slide 42: These are the listed indicators.

answers.body: Launching means defining boundaries, moving the module to a separate app and redirecting messages from in-process to cross-app.
answers.comment: L6, slide 43: The three steps listed.

answers.body: A module should become a satellite as soon as it has its own database table in the shared schema.
answers.comment: L6, slide 42: Size, traffic and a dedicated team are indicators; a table alone is not.

answers.body: The first satellite is easy and a modular monolith already solved authentication, messaging and data storage for it.
answers.comment: L6, slide 44: The first satellite is hard because it must solve exactly these concerns.

answers.body: No messages need to be redirected and modules in a monolith already communicate over the network.
answers.comment: L6, slide 43: In a monolith messages flow in-process and must be redirected to cross-app communication.

name: Select all observations that indicate you need MORE sophisticated domain modeling.

answers.body: Invariants keep breaking, and the same bug resurfaces in different places.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: Repeated broken invariants signal missing modeling of business rules.

answers.body: Features are described as tables and DTOs rather than domain concepts.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: Schema-driven thinking is a listed sign.

answers.body: Different teams use different terms for the same concept, so there is no shared language.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: Missing shared language is a listed sign.

answers.body: Heavy DDD is used for simple CRUD, with aggregates that wrap a few fields.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: This signals that modeling is already too complex.

answers.body: Stakeholders cannot follow the diagrams because the language has drifted from the business.
answers.comment: L6, slide 47: This signals that modeling is already too complex.

name: Select all correct statements about Domain Driven Design (DDD) as presented in the lecture.

answers.body: The main concept is that the domain object (aggregate root) is always valid.
answers.comment: L6, slide 53: Always-valid aggregate root is the main concept.

answers.body: There are no public setters and no mutable lists exposed; a collection is exposed as read-only while the list itself stays private.
answers.comment: L6, slide 55: No public setters on properties and no mutable lists.

answers.body: All changes come through public methods on the aggregate root, even when the change concerns an inner entity.
answers.comment: L6, slide 56: The root guards its own consistency.

answers.body: Inner entities of an aggregate may be modified directly by other aggregates for convenience.
answers.comment: L6, slides 56-57: Changes go through the aggregate root only.

answers.body: Aggregates in different domains communicate by calling each other's public methods directly.
answers.comment: L6, slide 57: Cross-domain communication is done via events.

name: Select all DDD terms that are matched with a correct description.

answers.body: Bounded context – a boundary within which a model and its language apply, e.g. Customer in a sales and a support context.
answers.comment: L6, slide 49: The slide shows Customer and Product in both a Sales and a Support Context (the one-line definition is general DDD wording).

answers.body: Domain event – something that happened in the domain (e.g. OrderStarted), handled by one or more event handlers.
answers.comment: L6, slides 52, 58: Events carry cross-domain communication.

answers.body: Aggregate root – the database table in which the aggregates of the system are stored with their inner entities.
answers.comment: L6, slide 50: The aggregate root is an entity through which the aggregate is accessed, not a table.

answers.body: Inner entity – an entity that other aggregates reference and modify directly, bypassing the aggregate root.
answers.comment: L6, slides 51, 56: Inner entities are changed only through the aggregate root.

name: A startup does not know whether its project will end in a year or live for ten. Select all recommendations that match “start simple, upgrade on pain”.

answers.body: It is OK to skip architecture or start simple for prototypes and hobby projects.
answers.comment: L6, slide 65: Starting small is fine for projects without further development plans.

answers.body: With an unknown future, start a little overkill with upgrade paths (e.g. clean architecture, modular monolith) and grow slowly.
answers.comment: L6, slides 38, 67-71: Uncertain future means a slightly overkill start, then upgrades.

answers.body: Start with DDD microservices for new projects, to avoid refactoring later when the project grows.
answers.comment: L6, slide 37: Microservices are not needed by most projects; complex starts suit high traffic, complex business and many teams.

answers.body: Starting very small is cheap and the architecture can be rewritten when pain appears.
answers.comment: L6, slide 67: Starting too small will kick you later; hence a slightly overkill start.

answers.body: Delay decisions about complexity until the project succeeds, then redesign it in one jump.
answers.comment: L6, slides 70-71: Increase complexity slowly and do not fear a slightly early jump.

name: A startup with three developers builds an internal booking system. Today it is mostly CRUD with a few business rules, but nobody knows whether the product will be dropped within a year or grow for ten years. Recommend an architecture along the three dimensions (code structure, deployment, problem modeling) and name the signals that would make you add or remove architecture later.
answer:
Principle: Fit the architecture to the problem and, because the future is unknown, “start simple, upgrade on pain”: start a little overkill with clear upgrade paths.
Code structure and deployment: Clean architecture (use cases that request dependencies through ports, adapters outside, persistence an afterthought) in a modular monolith (modules as if services, shared messages, hidden implementations) – not microservices. Add structure when merge conflicts concentrate in god files, ORM choices leak everywhere or onboarding is slow; remove it when trivial CRUD needs many layers/DTOs or tests are mostly mocks. Launch a satellite when a module becomes large, loaded with traffic or gets its own team.
Modeling: Start with use-case-oriented modeling; add DDD (always-valid aggregate roots, events between domains) when invariants keep breaking, features are described as tables/DTOs or teams use different terms for one concept; avoid heavy DDD for plain CRUD.
keyPoints: Fit complexity to the problem; start slightly overkill with upgrade paths
Deployment: modular monolith, no microservices yet; satellite signals
Modeling: use cases first, DDD only when invariants break or language drifts
Avoid heavy DDD and many layers for plain CRUD
Upgrade when real pain appears, not in advance
source: L6, slides 13-22, 27, 35-47, 53-57, 64-71; “use-case-oriented modeling first” is inferred from the complexity axis on slide 47 and from slide 70

name: The booking system runs as a modular monolith. Its Notifications module (e-mail and SMS) has grown large and self-sufficient, handles most of the traffic and is now looked after by a dedicated team. Plan how to turn it into a satellite: which of these facts are indicators, which steps you take in which order, what makes the first satellite difficult, and how the earlier modular design helps.
answer:
Indicators: All three facts from the scenario match: the module is large and self-sufficient, a large portion of traffic flows through it so more instances would help, and a team mainly handles it.
Steps: (1) Define the boundary of the module (which messages it receives and sends). (2) Move it into a separate application. (3) Redirect the messages that the rest of the system sends it from in-process to cross-application communication.
Hard parts of the first satellite: authentication between apps, messaging (choosing the right protocol, asynchronous execution) and data storage (its own data).
Why the design helps: modules were separate projects with shared message contracts and hidden implementations, so the boundary and the messages already exist and little code knows the internals; the “small village” (everyone knows everyone) would make this extraction painful.
keyPoints: All three facts match satellite indicators: size, traffic, dedicated team
Steps: define boundaries, move to separate app, redirect messages to cross-app
First satellite is hard: authentication, messaging, data storage
Shared messages and hidden implementation make the split easier
Everyone-knows-everyone coupling would make the split painful
